unit.title: The Jesus Lens
unit.summary: How to read the whole Bible with Jesus as the key: progressive revelation, how Jesus and Paul read the Scriptures, and how the Word made flesh interprets the hard texts, the types and shadows, and the prophecies. Each lesson gives the Jesus-lens reading its full voice and sets the other serious readings beside it.

lessons.title: Hard Texts: Violence, Accommodation and Changing Perception
lessons.question: The Bible says God ordered a massacre and then says God will punish it. He says something and we understand something. How do we read the violent parts of the Old Testament if Jesus shows us what God is like?
lessons.bigIdea: Every Christian reads the violent texts through some lens; the real questions are which lens, and how honestly we use it. One serious view says the Old Testament records a real but developing human perception of God that is corrected in Christ; other serious views say God truly commanded these things in a unique, limited setting, or that the canon deliberately leaves the tension open. Know all of them, and know that misused texts have cost real lives.

sections.heading: The problem stated honestly
sections.body:
The Old Testament contains passages where God is said to command or approve terrible violence. In Deuteronomy Israel is told to "utterly destroy" the nations of Canaan and to show them no mercy. In 1 Samuel 15 Saul is told to kill the Amalekites, "both man and woman, infant and suckling". A psalm blesses whoever dashes Babylon's babies against the rock. These are not obscure footnotes; they are in the text, and serious readers of every kind find them painful.

The learner put it this way: "He says something and we understand something." In other words, there is God's speaking, and there is how fallen people heard, understood and wrote it down. Whether that gap exists, how big it is, and how we can tell, is the real question of this lesson.

Jesus himself raises the issue. Asked about divorce, he says Moses allowed it "because of the hardness of your hearts: but from the beginning it was not so" (Matthew 19:8). So at least one law in the Torah was, by Jesus' own account, a concession to human hardness rather than a full picture of God's will. Every view in this lesson has to account for that verse.

sections.heading: One event, two verdicts: Jezreel
sections.body:
In 2 Kings 9–10 a prophet sent by Elisha anoints the army commander Jehu as king of Israel and tells him to strike down the house of Ahab, as judgement for the blood of the prophets and of Naboth. Jehu kills King Joram at Jezreel, has Jezebel thrown from a window, has seventy sons of Ahab beheaded, kills Ahab's officials, friends and priests, kills forty-two relatives of King Ahaziah of Judah, and then traps and slaughters the worshippers of Baal in their temple. Afterwards the narrator reports God saying: "Because thou hast done well in executing that which is right in mine eyes... thy children of the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel" (2 Kings 10:30). The very next verse adds that Jehu did not walk in God's law with all his heart and kept Jeroboam's golden calves.

About a century later, Hosea is told to name his son Jezreel, "for yet a little while, and I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu" (Hosea 1:4). The Hebrew verb is *paqad*, literally "visit": God will visit the bloodshed of Jezreel on Jehu's dynasty. Jehu's last descendant, Zechariah, was assassinated after six months on the throne (2 Kings 15:8-12), fulfilling both the promise of four generations and Hosea's warning.

So the same event receives what looks like praise in Kings and judgement in Hosea. The learner reads this as a change of lens: "What changed? Not God. The people writing about God developed better lenses. Hosea had the courage to say, 'No, that's not what God wanted.'" That is a real reading, held in various forms by Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak, Eric Seibert and Peter Enns. It is not the only reading. Many commentators argue that Hosea condemns not the commission but how Jehu carried it out: his ambition, his excess (killing Judah's princes and Ahab's friends went beyond the word to strike Ahab's house), and his later idolatry, which 2 Kings 10:31 already notes. Robert Chisholm argues that Hosea uses Jezreel as a pattern: as Jehu's house destroyed Ahab's house there, so Jehu's house will now fall. Others, like Peter Goeman, read "the blood of Jezreel" as the bloodshed's consequences rather than a verdict on Jehu's guilt. Critical scholars often explain the tension by sources: the Kings account comes from circles that celebrated Jehu's anti-Baal revolution; Hosea comes from a prophet who saw Jehu's dynasty as violent and corrupt. And some canonical readers say the Bible deliberately keeps both texts so that later readers learn that God's use of a human instrument is never a blank cheque. The widget below sets these readings side by side.

sections.heading: Accommodation: an old idea with new uses
sections.body:
"Accommodation" means that God adapts his communication to the capacity of the hearer, as a parent talks to a small child. The idea is ancient. Origen (3rd century) said that Scripture speaks of God's "anger" in the way we speak to children, not because God has human passions. John Chrysostom (late 4th century) spoke often of God's *synkatabasis*, his gracious "condescension" in coming down to our level. John Calvin wrote that God "lisps" to us as nurses do with infants (*Institutes* 1.13.1). Gregory of Nyssa found it unworthy of God that he would kill the innocent firstborn of Egypt for Pharaoh's sin, and read the story spiritually instead (*Life of Moses* 2.91-92).

Notice what these older uses usually meant. For most Fathers and for Calvin, accommodation concerned the *form* of revelation: human words, pictures of God with arms and anger, laws suited to a people's stage. It did not usually mean that God never commanded what the text says he commanded. Augustine, for example, defended the Old Testament wars as just, against the Manichaean Faustus (*Against Faustus* 22).

The modern "cruciform" version goes further. Greg Boyd (*The Crucifixion of the Warrior God*, 2017) argues that God, out of self-giving love, allowed his people to attribute to him violent actions that reflected their fallen, culturally conditioned views. On the cross Jesus bore our sin and appeared as a criminal; in the same way, Boyd says, God "stooped" to bear the ugly image his people projected onto him. Boyd still holds the whole Bible to be inspired: the violent portraits are inspired witnesses to how far God was willing to stoop. Eric Seibert (*Disturbing Divine Behavior*, 2009) distinguishes the "textual God" from the "actual God" revealed in Jesus. Brad Jersak (*A More Christlike God*, 2015) and Peter Enns (*The Bible Tells Me So*, 2014) make related moves. Supporters point to Matthew 19:8, to Ezekiel 20:25 ("I gave them also statutes that were not good"), and to Jeremiah 7:31, where God says child sacrifice "came not into my heart".

sections.heading: The conquest and herem: what are the options?
sections.body:
The Hebrew word *herem* ("devoted to destruction", often translated "utterly destroy") describes setting something apart for God by removing it completely from human use. In the conquest it is applied to Canaanite cities. Serious Christians read it in at least five ways.

(1) **Just judgement, as written.** God, the giver of life, judged nations whose sin had reached its full measure (Genesis 15:16; Leviticus 18:24-28), using Israel once, in a unique, unrepeatable moment. This is the traditional view of Augustine and many Reformed and evangelical scholars. (2) **Real command, but hyperbolic language.** Paul Copan and Matthew Flannagan (*Did God Really Command Genocide?*, 2014) argue that "utterly destroy" is stock war rhetoric in the ancient Near East, like a team that "slaughtered" its rival. The Moabite Stone (around 840 BC) claims that "Israel has utterly perished forever", which was plainly not true. In the Bible, too, Joshua 10:40 says all were destroyed, yet Judges 1 says the Canaanites remained, and Deuteronomy 7:2-3 forbids marrying the same people it says to destroy. On this reading the main goal was driving out and dismantling Canaanite religion, not killing every person. (3) **The "God I don't understand" view.** Christopher Wright admits there is no fully satisfying answer, holds that God did act in judgement, and stresses that the same God promises blessing to all nations and later threatens Israel with the same judgement. David Lamb (*God Behaving Badly*, 2011) shows how much mercy surrounds the hard texts. (4) **Cruciform reinterpretation.** Boyd: Israel heard God's call to possess the land through their violent culture; the cross shows us what God was really like behind that portrait. (5) **Textual God vs actual God.** Seibert and Enns: these are Israel's stories, told the way ancient peoples told war stories, and Christians are not obliged to believe God acted that way.

John and Harvey Walton (*The Lost World of the Israelite Conquest*, 2017) add a further angle: *herem* was about removing a people's identity and order, not about punishing their guilt, which changes the moral question again.

sections.heading: Psalm 137, Elijah's fire and Jesus' rebuke
sections.body:
Psalm 137 is the cry of exiles who watched Jerusalem burn. It ends: "Happy shall he be, that taketh and dasheth thy little ones against the stones." Most readers today, of every view, agree that this is an honest prayer of rage handed over to God rather than a command to imitate. The Bible lets traumatised people speak in their own voice. Origen read it allegorically: the "little ones of Babylon" are the first sinful thoughts in the soul, to be dashed against the rock who is Christ (*Against Celsus* 7.22).

In 2 Kings 1 Elijah calls down fire on soldiers sent to arrest him. In Luke 9, when a Samaritan village refuses Jesus, James and John ask, "wilt thou that we command fire to come down from heaven, and consume them, even as Elias did?" Jesus turns and rebukes them. Many later manuscripts add, "Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of. For the Son of man is not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them" (KJV Luke 9:55-56). These words are missing from the earliest manuscripts, so modern translations put them in a footnote, but the rebuke itself is in all of them. Jesus-lens readers see here a model: Jesus refuses to repeat an Old Testament act that his disciples assumed was a pattern to follow. Other readers answer that Jesus rebukes the disciples' spirit and their misreading of their own mission, not Elijah's prophetic act in its own time.

In the same way, in Luke 4 Jesus reads Isaiah 61 in the synagogue and stops just before "the day of vengeance of our God". Jesus-lens readers find that pause significant; others note that Jesus speaks of judgement elsewhere (Luke 13:1-5; Luke 21:20-24).

sections.heading: Why this matters: violence done in the name of Scripture
sections.body:
The learner wrote: "Without the Word (Jesus) the Bible becomes deadly. Much violence has taken place in the name of Scripture." History bears this out, and it should be told briefly and accurately.

The First Crusade (preached in 1095) was framed as holy war and pilgrimage; some chroniclers described the slaughter in Jerusalem in 1099 with biblical language. In the Spanish conquest of the Americas, the *Requerimiento* (1513) was read to native peoples demanding submission to the Church and Crown, and in the Valladolid debate (1550–1551) Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda defended the wars partly with Old Testament precedents, while Bartolomé de las Casas answered from the Gospel. Some English Puritan writers in New England described Native Americans with Canaanite and Amalekite imagery. Defenders of slavery in the American South cited the "curse of Ham" (really a curse on Canaan, Genesis 9:25) and the household codes; Thornton Stringfellow's *Scriptural Testimony* (1841) is one example. In South Africa, parts of the Dutch Reformed Church built a theological case for apartheid from Babel and the separation of nations (Genesis 11; Acts 17:26); in 1982 the World Alliance of Reformed Churches declared that defence a heresy, and the Belhar Confession answered it.

These abuses do not by themselves decide which reading of the conquest is right: defenders of the traditional view insist that the conquest was unique and never a licence for later wars, and they point out that Christians who opposed slavery and apartheid also argued from Scripture. But every view must answer this: if a text has been used to kill, how do we read it so that it cannot be used that way again? The Jesus lens says: by Jesus. Traditional readers say: by careful attention to covenant and context, which also leads to Jesus. Both agree the Bible read without Christ and without love has been dangerous.

visuals.title: Jezreel: two verdicts, five readings
visuals.intro: 2 Kings 10:30 commends Jehu's purge of Ahab's house. Hosea 1:4 announces judgement on Jehu's house for "the blood of Jezreel". Read the two verses side by side, then through each lens.
visuals.passage:
2 Kings 10:30: "And the LORD said unto Jehu, Because thou hast done well in executing that which is right in mine eyes, and hast done unto the house of Ahab according to all that was in mine heart, thy children of the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel."

Hosea 1:4: "And the LORD said unto him, Call his name Jezreel; for yet a little while, and I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and will cause to cease the kingdom of the house of Israel." (KJV)

lenses.name: Developing lenses (the learner's reading)
lenses.who: The learner; in related forms Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak, Eric Seibert, Peter Enns, Brian Zahnd
lenses.reading: God did not change; Israel's perception of God did. The writer of Kings understood Jehu's bloodbath as God's will. Hosea, a century later, saw more clearly and said the massacre was not what God wanted. The canon keeps both so that we can watch the lens being corrected, a movement that is completed in Jesus, who refuses violence. Strength: it takes the contradiction at face value. Critique: 2 Kings 9:6-10 has a prophet commission Jehu in God's name, and Hosea himself announces violent judgement on Israel, so Hosea is not a pacifist corrective.

lenses.name: Commission obeyed, but in the wrong spirit
lenses.who: Many traditional commentators (e.g. the Catholic Haydock commentary; many evangelical commentaries)
lenses.reading: God did use Jehu to judge Ahab's house, and the act itself is commended. But Jehu went beyond the commission (killing Judah's royal family and Ahab's friends and priests), acted from ambition, and kept the golden calves (2 Kings 10:29-31). Hosea condemns the bloodshed as Jehu actually carried it out. Strength: it explains why 2 Kings 10:31 already qualifies the praise. Critique: Hosea 1:4 does not mention excess or motives; this explanation is brought in from outside.

lenses.name: Jezreel as a pattern of judgement
lenses.who: Robert B. Chisholm Jr. (Bibliotheca Sacra, 2019); Peter Goeman
lenses.reading: Hosea is not reversing Kings. "Visit the blood of Jezreel on the house of Jehu" means that what happened to Ahab's house at Jezreel will now happen to Jehu's house, because it has become just as corrupt. The name Jezreel recalls the place of a dynasty's fall. Strength: it keeps both texts true without a contradiction. Critique: the plain sense of "avenge the blood" (KJV) suggests guilt for bloodshed, and many translations read it that way.

lenses.name: Different sources, different politics
lenses.who: Historical-critical scholarship (common in standard critical commentaries)
lenses.reading: 2 Kings 9–10 comes from circles that celebrated Jehu's revolution against the Baal-worshipping Omride dynasty. Hosea, an eighth-century prophet in the north, saw the Jehu dynasty's violence as the root of Israel's ruin. The texts disagree because their authors disagreed. Strength: it is honest about genuine human voices in Scripture. Critique: by itself it says little about how a believing community should hear God through both texts.

lenses.name: Deliberate canonical tension
lenses.who: Canonical and narrative readers (e.g. in the line of Brevard Childs; many Jewish readers who prize argument within Scripture)
lenses.reading: The editors who gathered the Scriptures knew both texts and kept both on purpose. Together they teach that God may use a human instrument without endorsing everything the instrument does, and that a prophet's verdict can expose what a court history celebrated. The tension is a lesson, not a mistake. Strength: it respects the final shape of Scripture. Critique: critics on both sides say it can avoid deciding what God actually wanted.

visuals.title: Approaches to violence in the Old Testament
visuals.intro: Each position is held by serious, believing (or in some cases academic) readers. Place your own view, and read the strongest case for the views furthest from you.
visuals.left: God commanded it as written, and it was just
visuals.right: The text reflects human misperception of God, corrected in Christ

stops.label: Just judgement as written
stops.who: Augustine (Against Faustus 22); many Reformed and evangelical scholars, e.g. Clay Jones, Eugene Merrill
stops.text: God is the Lord of life and judge of all. The Canaanites' sin had reached its full measure (Gen 15:16). The conquest was a unique, limited act of judgement, never a model for later wars. Critique: it is hard to reconcile the killing of infants with Jesus' revelation of God; defenders answer that God takes infants to himself and that our moral sense is itself shaped by God's revelation.

stops.label: Real command, hyperbolic language
stops.who: Paul Copan and Matthew Flannagan; Nicholas Wolterstorff (on hyperbole)
stops.text: God did command Israel to dispossess the Canaanites, but "leave nothing alive" is ancient war rhetoric. The main targets were military strongholds and Canaanite religion, and the biblical text itself shows survivors. Critique: 1 Samuel 15 and Joshua 6 seem specific, and hyperbole still leaves God commanding killing.

stops.label: Real but troubling: the God I don't understand
stops.who: Christopher J. H. Wright; David T. Lamb; John and Harvey Walton (on herem)
stops.text: Hold the conquest within the whole story: judgement on sin, God's same judgement later on Israel, and a promise to bless all nations. Admit what we cannot explain. Critique: some find this honest but unresolved; others say it is the only honest place to stand.

stops.label: Cruciform reinterpretation
stops.who: Greg Boyd (The Crucifixion of the Warrior God); Brad Jersak; Brian Zahnd
stops.text: The whole Bible is inspired, but the cross is the lens. Where a portrait of God contradicts the crucified Christ, it shows God stooping to bear his people's fallen views, as he bore our sin on the cross. Critique: who decides which portraits are fallen? Jesus himself affirms Old Testament judgement stories (Matt 24:37-39) and the New Testament contains judgement too.

stops.label: Textual God vs actual God
stops.text: These are Israel's own stories, told the way ancient peoples told war stories. We may honour them as Scripture without believing God actually did these things. Jesus is the standard. Critique: it can make the reader the judge of Scripture and risks the old error of Marcion, who split the God of Israel from the Father of Jesus.

stops.label: Purely human texts
stops.who: Many secular and critical scholars (e.g. Hector Avalos)
stops.text: The texts are human products reflecting ancient nationalism and should be judged by modern ethics. No divine meaning is sought. Critique (from believers of every view): it does not read the Bible as Scripture at all, and it cannot explain why the same texts produced the prophets' and Jesus' ethic of love for enemies.

visuals.title: How the church has handled violent texts
visuals.intro: A short, selective history. Some dates are approximate.

events.label: Marcion rejected
events.text: Marcion taught that the violent God of the Old Testament was a lesser god than the Father of Jesus. The church at Rome rejected him and kept the Old Testament as Christian Scripture.

events.label: Origen, Against Celsus
events.text: Origen answers a pagan critic: God's "wrath" is accommodated language, and Psalm 137 and other violent texts are to be read spiritually (Against Celsus 4.71-72; 7.22).

events.label: Gregory of Nyssa
events.text: In The Life of Moses Gregory finds the killing of Egypt's innocent firstborn unworthy of God if read only literally, and reads it as the destruction of evil at its beginning.

events.label: Augustine, Against Faustus
events.text: Augustine defends the Old Testament wars as just acts commanded by God against the Manichaean critic Faustus; this becomes the main Western view.

events.label: First Crusade preached
events.text: Pope Urban II preaches the Crusade at Clermont. Holy-war language, partly drawn from the Old Testament, is applied to a new war.

events.label: Valladolid debate
events.text: Sepúlveda defends the Spanish wars in the Americas partly with Old Testament precedents; Las Casas argues from the Gospel for peaceful conversion.

events.label: Calvin's final Institutes
events.text: Calvin's teaching on accommodation (God "lisps" to us, Institutes 1.13.1) shapes Protestant reading, though he still holds the commands to be God's.

events.label: Slavery defended from Scripture
events.text: Thornton Stringfellow and others defend American slavery from Genesis 9 and the household codes; abolitionists answer from Scripture too.

events.label: Apartheid theology declared heresy
events.text: The World Alliance of Reformed Churches declares the biblical defence of apartheid a heresy; the Belhar Confession is drafted the same year.

events.label: Seibert, Disturbing Divine Behavior
events.text: Distinguishes the "textual God" from the "actual God" revealed in Jesus.

events.label: Copan, Is God a Moral Monster?
events.text: A popular defence of the Old Testament ethic, later developed with Flannagan in Did God Really Command Genocide? (2014).

events.label: Boyd, The Crucifixion of the Warrior God
events.text: A two-volume case for a cruciform hermeneutic: the cross as the lens for every portrait of God.

voices.text: If a reading of Scripture gives you a Father who is unlike the Son, your reading is incorrect.
voices.source: quoted in the learner's course notes

voices.text: As nurses commonly do with infants, God is wont in a measure to 'lisp' in speaking to us.
voices.source: Institutes of the Christian Religion 1.13.1 (Beveridge translation)

views.name: Developing perception, corrected in Christ (the Jesus lens)
views.who: Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak, Brian Zahnd, Eric Seibert, Peter Enns, Bill Johnson's "Jesus is perfect theology"; the learner
views.summary: God has always been like Jesus. The Old Testament is an inspired, honest record of a people's real but developing and often flawed perception of that God. God accommodated himself to their violent, tribal world (Matt 19:8) to lead them on, and allowed his reputation to be marred by their portraits. Jesus, the exact imprint of God's nature (Heb 1:3) and his "exegesis" (John 1:18), shows who God has been all along. Jesus modelled this himself: "You have heard that it was said... but I say to you" (Matt 5:38-44).
views.strengths: It takes the moral problem seriously instead of explaining it away. It makes Jesus, not a single verse, the final word about God. It has precedent in the Fathers' unease with literal readings, and the canon itself shows development (Hosea on Jezreel, Ezek 20:25, Jer 7:31). It guards against using Scripture to justify violence.
views.critiques: Jesus affirmed the Old Testament strongly (Matt 5:17-18; John 10:35) and treated its judgement stories as real (Luke 17:26-32). The New Testament also contains divine judgement (Acts 5:1-11; 2 Thess 1:6-9; Rev 19:11-16). Who decides what is "Christlike"? There is a risk of shaping Jesus in our own image and drifting toward Marcion. Boyd answers that he keeps every text as inspired; critics reply that calling a text an inspired record of error is still a major change.

views.name: Just judgement in a unique moment
views.who: Augustine; much of the Reformed and evangelical tradition (e.g. Eugene Merrill in Show Them No Mercy, 2003; Clay Jones)
views.summary: God, who gives life, has the right to take it. The conquest was judgement on long-tolerated evil (Gen 15:16; Lev 18:24-28), limited to one land and one time, and the same God later judged Israel by the same standard. It is not a model for anyone today. The cross does not cancel God's justice; it shows that he bore it himself.
views.strengths: It accepts the text as it stands and fits Jesus' high view of Scripture. It holds that love and judgement belong together in both Testaments. It keeps God's moral authority above ours.
views.critiques: It struggles with the killing of children and with how such texts have been used. Jesus-lens readers say it lets the Old Testament picture define God and then fits Jesus into it, rather than the reverse.

views.name: Real command, hyperbolic rhetoric
views.who: Paul Copan (Is God a Moral Monster?, 2011); Copan and Matthew Flannagan (Did God Really Command Genocide?, 2014)
views.summary: God did command Israel to take the land, but "utterly destroy" and "leave nothing alive" are stock ancient war rhetoric, as other ancient inscriptions show. The Bible itself reports survivors in the same land. The focus was on driving out and ending Canaanite religion, not killing every person.
views.strengths: It reads the texts in their ancient setting and answers modern objections without abandoning inerrancy. It notices real tensions inside Joshua and Judges.
views.critiques: Some passages (1 Sam 15:3) seem deliberately specific. Even hyperbolic language still has God commanding killing. Critical scholars say the hyperbole argument is selective.

views.name: Canonical tension and dialogue
views.who: Canonical readers; many Jewish interpreters who value argument within Scripture; Walter Brueggemann ("testimony and counter-testimony")
views.summary: The Bible is not one flat voice but a conversation. Kings and Hosea, Joshua and Ruth, Nahum and Jonah answer each other. The community is meant to hear both and to argue faithfully, as Abraham argued with God (Gen 18:25).
views.strengths: It honours the real shape of Scripture and the long Jewish tradition of holy argument. It avoids forcing either a harmonised or a corrected reading.
views.critiques: It may leave believers without guidance on what God is actually like. Jesus-lens readers say the conversation has an ending: Jesus. Traditional readers say it can weaken the authority of each text.

misreadings.topic: "The Old Testament God is angry; the New Testament God is loving"
misreadings.popular: Many church members assume that the Old Testament shows a wrathful God and the New Testament a gentle one, as if God changed at Bethlehem.
misreadings.inContext: Both Testaments speak of God as merciful (Exod 34:6-7; Jonah 4:2; Ps 103:8-13) and both speak of judgement (Matt 23:33; Rev 19:11-16). The Jesus-lens view does not say God changed; it says people's perception of the same God developed and was completed in Jesus. That is a different claim, and its holders reject the "two Gods" idea as firmly as anyone.
misreadings.defence: Traditional scholars agree the two-Gods picture is false: the early church condemned it in Marcion. They add that the cross itself shows God's justice and love together, so wrath is not simply removed in the New Testament.
misreadings.whyItMatters: If we set the Testaments against each other we lose half the Bible, and we lose the Jewish Scriptures that Jesus himself read and loved.

misreadings.topic: "Accommodation" always meant what the cruciform view means
misreadings.popular: Some readers assume that Calvin and the Church Fathers taught that God's violent commands were really human misunderstandings.
misreadings.inContext: Most Fathers and Calvin used accommodation for the form of revelation (human language, images of God's anger, laws suited to Israel's stage). Some, like Origen and Gregory of Nyssa, did refuse literal readings of certain violent texts and read them spiritually. Boyd and others build on these strands but take a further step.
misreadings.defence: Traditional scholars stress that Augustine and Calvin both held the commands to be genuinely God's. Cruciform writers reply that the Fathers' unease with the literal sense shows they felt the same problem.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Using historical names accurately keeps the conversation honest and lets each side see what is old and what is new in its own position.

discuss: Read 2 Kings 10:28-31 and Hosea 1:4 aloud. Which of the five readings in the lenses widget seems strongest to you, and what would most weaken it?
Jesus says Moses allowed divorce "because of the hardness of your hearts" (Matt 19:8). Are there other Old Testament laws or actions you think fall under the same principle? How would you know?
What is the difference between saying "God changed" and "our perception of God changed"? Why does the difference matter?
If someone says, "Who decides what is Christlike?", how would you answer from the Gospels rather than from your own preferences?
Psalm 137 puts a terrible prayer into the Bible. What might it teach about bringing anger to God rather than acting on it?
The Crusades, slavery and apartheid were all defended from Scripture. What safeguards in how we read could have helped Christians then, and what might we be missing now?
practice: Read 2 Kings 9–10 in one sitting, then Hosea 1. Write down every point where the two seem to agree and every point where they seem to disagree.

Take one hard text (for example 1 Samuel 15 or Psalm 137) and write a one-paragraph reading of it from two different positions on the spectrum. Try to make the view you disagree with sound as strong as its best defenders would.
Read Matthew 5:38-48 slowly each morning this week and ask: what does this tell me about what God is like?

lessons.title: Types and Shadows
lessons.question: What does the Bible mean when it calls the Old Testament a "shadow" of Christ, and how do we find types without making things up?
lessons.bigIdea: A type is a real person, event or institution in Israel's history that God shaped to foreshadow a greater fulfilment in Christ, the antitype. Shadows are real, but the body that casts them is Christ (Col 2:17). Good typology starts from real history and the New Testament's own patterns; fanciful typology starts from the reader's imagination.

sections.heading: Shadow and body
sections.body:
Paul tells the Colossians not to let anyone judge them about food, festivals, new moons or sabbaths, "which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ" (Colossians 2:16-17). A shadow is real; it has the shape of the thing that casts it. But you would not hug someone's shadow when the person is standing in front of you.

Hebrews uses the same picture. The priests serve "unto the example and shadow of heavenly things" (Hebrews 8:5), and "the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things" (Hebrews 10:1). The tabernacle was built from a pattern shown to Moses on the mountain (Exodus 25:40). The earthly copy points to the heavenly reality, which Christ has now entered.

Tommy Miller, quoted in the learner's notes, put it this way: you can find "types, shadows, poems, and dreams across the Old Testament. But the Father's face is fully revealed in the Son's face." Typology is one of the main ways the New Testament shows that the Old Testament is Part One of a single story whose centre is Jesus.

sections.heading: Type and antitype: the words
sections.body:
The Greek word *typos* first meant the mark left by a blow, then an impression, a pattern or model. Paul calls Adam "the figure (*typos*) of him that was to come" (Romans 5:14), and says the wilderness events "happened unto them for ensamples (*typoi*)" and "were written for our admonition" (1 Corinthians 10:6, 10:11). Peter calls baptism the *antitypon* of Noah's flood (1 Peter 3:21): the thing that answers to the earlier pattern.

So a **type** is the earlier, real person, event or institution; the **antitype** is the later and greater fulfilment. Most scholars name two marks of a true type. First, **historical correspondence**: there is a real likeness between the two, not just a shared word. Second, **escalation**: the antitype is greater. Jesus is not just another Jonah: "a greater than Jonas is here" (Matthew 12:41). He is not just another temple: "in this place is one greater than the temple" (Matthew 12:6).

Typology is different from allegory. Allegory treats details of a text as symbols of spiritual ideas, often without regard for the history (for example, reading the five stones David picked up as five virtues). Typology says the history itself matters: God really did bring Israel through the sea, and that real event was shaped to point beyond itself. Paul once calls his reading of Hagar and Sarah an allegory (Galatians 4:24), which shows the line between the two was not as sharp in the first century as modern textbooks make it.

sections.heading: Jesus taught the church to read this way
sections.body:
On the road to Emmaus, "beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself" (Luke 24:27). He told the leaders, "Search the scriptures... they are they which testify of me" (John 5:39). He compared his lifting up on the cross to Moses lifting up the bronze serpent (John 3:14), his body to the temple (John 2:19-21), and himself to the manna from heaven (John 6:32-35).

The early church followed. Paul calls Christ "our passover" (1 Corinthians 5:7) and "the last Adam" (1 Corinthians 15:45). Matthew presents Jesus as a new Moses and a new Israel: a child rescued from a murderous king, called out of Egypt, tested forty days in the wilderness, giving the law from a mountain. Hebrews reads the priesthood, sacrifices and Day of Atonement as one long shadow of Christ's work.

Richard Hays calls this "reading backwards": after the resurrection, the disciples reread their Scriptures and saw patterns they had not seen before. The patterns were really there; the light by which they were seen was new. This is exactly what the Jesus lens claims: Jesus is the context and life of the Scriptures.

sections.heading: Guardrails: how to avoid fanciful typology
sections.body:
Typology has been used brilliantly and badly. In the Middle Ages almost every object in the tabernacle and every detail of the Song of Songs was given a Christ-meaning, often with little control. In reaction, the Anglican bishop Herbert Marsh (early 19th century) argued that only types explicitly named in the New Testament should be accepted. Most interpreters today stand between these poles.

Helpful guardrails: (1) **Start with the history.** What did this mean to its first readers? A type is never less than its own story. (2) **Look for real correspondence**, not a shared colour or number. (3) **Look for escalation** toward Christ and his people. (4) **Let the New Testament lead.** Types it names (Adam, Passover, manna, the serpent, Jonah, the temple, Melchizedek) are the clearest; patterns it follows (exodus, new creation, the suffering righteous one) can be traced further with care. (5) **Do not build doctrine on a type alone.** A type illustrates and confirms what Scripture teaches plainly elsewhere; it should not carry a teaching no clear text supports. (6) **Check with the church's reading.** If no one in the history of the church has seen your type, ask why.

These guardrails do not quench the joy of discovery. They keep the shadow attached to the body.

sections.heading: Types and the hard texts
sections.body:
Types connect directly to the previous lesson. If Joshua is a type of Jesus (they share the same Hebrew name, Yehoshua), what kind of conquest does the greater Joshua lead? The New Testament answers: a conquest of the powers of sin and death by self-giving love (Colossians 2:15; Ephesians 6:12). Christ leads his people into the true "rest" that Joshua could not give (Hebrews 4:8-9).

Jesus-lens readers argue that this shows the direction of the whole Bible: the shadow of holy war becomes the body of the cross, where Christ "made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it". Traditional readers agree that the conquest points to Christ's victory, but hold that the earlier war was itself a real act of divine judgement which the cross does not deny. Both read Joshua through Jesus; they differ on what the shadow was in its own time.

visuals.title: Type and antitype
visuals.intro: Each row is a type the New Testament itself names or clearly follows. Notice the correspondence and the escalation.

Baptism

Jesus the bread of life

Looking in trust at what is lifted up brings life

Christ's body; the church; the new creation
God dwells with his people
From a tent in one place to God dwelling in his people everywhere

visuals.title: Type, allegory or over-reach?
visuals.intro: Sort each reading. Is it a type with real historical correspondence, an allegorical reading (spiritual meaning given to details), or an over-reach that the guardrails would warn against?

items.text: Adam is a figure of Christ: one man's act affects all humanity.
items.why: Paul names it as a type (typos), with real correspondence and escalation.

items.text: The bronze serpent lifted up points to Jesus lifted up on the cross.
items.why: Jesus himself makes the connection; the pattern of looking and living is real.

items.text: Hagar and Sarah stand for two covenants, Sinai and the Jerusalem above.
items.why: Paul himself uses the word "allegory" (allēgoroumena). He gives the story a symbolic meaning for his argument.

items.text: The little ones of Babylon in Psalm 137 are the first sinful thoughts, to be dashed against Christ the rock.
items.why: Origen's spiritual reading (Against Celsus 7.22). It is a moral allegory, not a historical type.

items.text: Rahab's scarlet cord is a picture of the saving blood of Christ.
items.why: Clement of Rome and later Fathers read it this way. The New Testament praises Rahab's faith (Heb 11:31) but does not draw this link, so it is best treated as a devotional, allegorical reading.

items.text: The 153 fish in John 21 prove that a secret number code runs through the whole Bible.
items.why: Many symbolic meanings have been suggested for 153, but building a hidden code system on one number breaks the guardrails: no clear text supports it.

items.text: Because Joseph's coat had many colours, every colour in the tabernacle predicts a doctrine.
items.why: A shared feature (colour) is not historical correspondence, and the reading builds teaching that no clear text supports.

items.text: Israel called out of Egypt is fulfilled in Jesus returning from Egypt.
items.why: Matthew presents Jesus as the true Israel, God's son, retracing Israel's story (Hos 11:1).

visuals.title: How far should typology go?
visuals.left: Only the types the New Testament names
visuals.right: Every detail can point to Christ

stops.label: Marsh's rule
stops.who: Herbert Marsh (Anglican bishop, early 19th century) and some later evangelicals
stops.text: Accept only types explicitly identified in the New Testament. Safe and controlled, but critics say it ignores the patterns the apostles taught us to see.

stops.label: Patterns the New Testament teaches
stops.who: Leonhard Goppelt; Patrick Fairbairn; Richard Davidson; most evangelical scholars today
stops.text: The New Testament gives both named types and a way of reading (exodus, temple, king, new creation). We may follow those patterns with historical correspondence and escalation as tests.

stops.label: Reading backwards
stops.who: Richard Hays; many Catholic and Orthodox readers
stops.text: After the resurrection the whole Old Testament is reread in Christ's light, as the disciples did on the Emmaus road. Figural reading is a gift, guided by the church's tradition.

stops.label: Fuller allegorical reading
stops.who: Origen; much medieval exegesis (the four senses of Scripture)
stops.text: Every detail can carry spiritual meaning, alongside the literal sense. Rich and devotional, but critics, from the Antiochene Fathers to the Reformers, warned that it can lose the history and let readers find whatever they want.

voices.text: The New is in the Old concealed; the Old is in the New revealed.
You can find types, shadows, poems, and dreams across the Old Testament. But the Father's face is fully revealed in the Son's face.
voices.source: quoted in the learner's course notes

views.name: Christ-centred typology
views.who: The Jesus-lens tradition; Tommy Miller; Greg Boyd; many Reformed preachers (e.g. Edmund Clowney, Graeme Goldsworthy)
views.summary: Because Jesus said all the Scriptures testify of him (John 5:39; Luke 24:27), every part of the Old Testament finds its meaning in him. Types are not decorations; they show that the Old Testament is Part One of one story, and that the Father who seemed hidden in shadows is fully seen in the Son.
views.strengths: It follows Jesus' and the apostles' own practice. It keeps the Old Testament central for Christians and shows its unity.
views.critiques: It can rush past the first meaning of a text to reach Christ, and can make every sermon sound the same. Jewish readers note that it can erase the text's own meaning for Israel.

views.name: Controlled, history-first typology
views.who: Leonhard Goppelt (Typos, 1939); Richard Davidson (Typology in Scripture, 1981); many evangelical scholars
views.summary: Typology is real and important, but is controlled by two tests: historical correspondence and escalation. Start with the text's own meaning; let the New Testament's named types and patterns guide further readings.
views.strengths: It keeps typology honest and teachable. It respects the original history and avoids fanciful readings.
views.critiques: Those who value the Fathers say it can be too narrow and miss the richness of the church's figural reading.

views.name: Figural reading within the church's tradition
views.who: Catholic and Orthodox traditions; Henri de Lubac; Richard Hays (Echoes of Scripture in the Gospels, 2016)
views.summary: The Fathers' spiritual reading is a gift. Within the boundaries of the faith of the church (the "rule of faith"), readers may see Christ in many details, as the liturgy does in Holy Week and Easter readings.
views.strengths: It is deeply rooted in history and worship. It joins head and heart.
views.critiques: Protestant critics say it can let tradition, rather than the text, decide meaning. Historical critics say it reads later beliefs into older texts.

views.name: Jewish and historical-critical caution
views.who: Jewish interpreters (e.g. Jon Levenson); many critical scholars
views.summary: The Hebrew Bible has its own meaning for Israel, which must not be swallowed by Christian readings. Christian typology is a later community's way of reading, not what the original authors meant.
views.strengths: It protects the first meaning and reminds Christians that these are Israel's Scriptures too.
views.critiques: Christians answer that Jesus and the apostles were Jews reading their own Scriptures this way, and that Jewish tradition also reads patterns (for example, the exodus as a pattern for future redemption, Isa 43:16-19).

misreadings.popular: Some preaching treats any detail (a colour, a number, a piece of wood) as a hidden picture of Jesus, and builds teachings on it.
misreadings.inContext: In the New Testament, types are real events and persons whose history matters: the Passover really happened; Jonah's story is told as history. The connection is in the pattern of God's saving acts, not in random details.
misreadings.defence: Careful scholars of every tradition agree. The Fathers themselves debated this (Alexandria favoured allegory, Antioch insisted on history), and the Reformers pushed back against medieval excesses.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Fanciful typology makes the Bible a puzzle for clever readers and opens the door to almost any teaching. Sound typology shows the deep unity of one story.

misreadings.topic: "If it is a shadow, it does not matter"
misreadings.popular: Some Christians conclude that since the law and the feasts were shadows, the Old Testament is now irrelevant.
misreadings.inContext: A shadow has the real shape of what casts it. The feasts, temple and sacrifices teach what Christ's work means; the New Testament explains Christ through them. Jesus came to fulfil the law and prophets, not to abolish them (Matt 5:17).
misreadings.defence: Traditional and Jesus-lens readers agree here: the Old Testament is made eternally relevant by its fulfilment. They differ on which Old Testament practices still bind Christians, but not on its value.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Without the shadows we cannot understand words like "Lamb of God", "high priest" and "atonement".

discuss: Colossians 2:17 says the shadows belong to "things to come" but the body is Christ. What difference does that make to how you read Leviticus?
Pick a type from the compare table. What is the correspondence, and what is the escalation?
Why do you think Paul calls his reading of Hagar and Sarah an "allegory"? Does that give us permission to allegorise freely, or not?
Which guardrail do you think is most often ignored in preaching you have heard?
How might a Jewish reader feel about Christian typology? How can Christians read typologically while still honouring the text's meaning for Israel?
practice: Read Hebrews 9 alongside Leviticus 16. List each element of the Day of Atonement and what Hebrews says it points to.

Choose one Old Testament story you love. Write its meaning for its first readers first, then ask whether the New Testament treats it as a type. If not, ask whether a pattern the New Testament follows applies.
Read Luke 24:13-35 and imagine walking that road. Which Old Testament passages do you think Jesus explained?

lessons.title: Prophecy: Fulfilled, Dual, Conditional and Patterned
lessons.question: How do prophecies work? Some are fulfilled once, some seem to be fulfilled twice, some never happen because people repent, and some are used in a general way: "this is that". How do we tell which is which?
lessons.bigIdea: Biblical prophecy is first a word from God to his people about their covenant life (forth-telling), and only sometimes a prediction (foretelling). When it predicts, it may be fulfilled directly, fulfilled more than once, cancelled by repentance, or filled full as a pattern that reaches its climax in Jesus. Recognising the kind of prophecy keeps us from both cynicism and sensationalism.

sections.heading: Forth-telling before foretelling
sections.body:
In popular thinking a prophet is someone who predicts the future. In the Bible, a prophet is first someone who speaks for God to his people now. Amos cries, "let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream" (Amos 5:24). Micah sums up what God requires: "to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God" (Micah 6:8). This is **forth-telling**: speaking God's word into the present, calling people back to covenant faithfulness.

**Foretelling**, predicting what is to come, is part of prophecy, but a smaller part than most people think. Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart estimate that less than 2 percent of Old Testament prophecy is messianic, less than 5 percent describes the new-covenant age, and less than 1 percent concerns events still future to us (*How to Read the Bible for All Its Worth*). Most of it addresses Israel and the nations in the prophets' own day.

In the New Testament, Paul says the one who prophesies speaks "to edification, and exhortation, and comfort" (1 Corinthians 14:3), and that prophecy must be weighed (1 Corinthians 14:29; 1 Thessalonians 5:20-21). And Revelation gives the centre of it all: "the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy" (Revelation 19:10).

sections.heading: Fulfilled and dual (or multiple) fulfilment
sections.body:
Some prophecies point to a single fulfilment. Micah 5:2 names Bethlehem as the birthplace of a ruler whose origins are "from of old", and Matthew cites it for Jesus' birth (Matthew 2:5-6).

Others seem to be fulfilled more than once. **Isaiah 7:14** is the famous example. King Ahaz is terrified of two invading kings. Isaiah gives a sign: a young woman (Hebrew *almah*) will conceive and bear a son called Immanuel, and before the child is old enough to choose good and evil, those two kings' lands will be deserted (Isaiah 7:16). That sign had to mean something to Ahaz in his own lifetime. Yet Matthew 1:22-23, following the Greek translation that has *parthenos* ("virgin"), sees its full meaning in Jesus' virgin birth: God truly with us. Many evangelical scholars call this a dual fulfilment; others say Isaiah 7–11 as a whole already looks beyond Ahaz to a royal child (Isaiah 9:6-7), so Matthew reads the passage as a unit. The word "dual" is a label, not a biblical term; some prefer "near and far" or "typological" fulfilment.

Other examples: God's promise to David of a son whose throne would last for ever (2 Samuel 7:12-16) applies to Solomon and is applied to Jesus (Hebrews 1:5). Jesus' words in Matthew 24 mix the destruction of the temple in AD 70 with his final coming, and interpreters still debate how to divide them. Prophets often saw future events like mountain peaks from far away: two peaks that look side by side may in fact be far apart.

sections.heading: Patterned fulfilment: "this is that"
sections.body:
At Pentecost Peter says, "this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel" (Acts 2:16, KJV). He quotes Joel 2:28-32, and even changes Joel's "afterward" to "in the last days". Some details, like the moon turning to blood, did not visibly happen that morning. Peter is not claiming every line was ticked off; he is saying, "this outpouring is the thing Joel spoke about; the last days have begun." Jewish interpreters of the time used a similar "this is" method: the Dead Sea Scrolls' commentary on Habakkuk says, in effect, "this refers to" events in their own community.

**Hosea 11:1** is the clearest case of pattern. "When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt." In Hosea this is not a prediction at all; it looks back to the exodus. Yet Matthew writes that Jesus' return from Egypt happened "that it might be fulfilled" (Matthew 2:15). Matthew's word "fulfil" (*plēroō*) means "fill full". Jesus relives Israel's story: God's son, out of Egypt, through the waters, tested in the wilderness, faithful where Israel failed. The pattern is filled to the brim in him. Matthew 2:17-18 does the same with Jeremiah 31:15, Rachel weeping for her children.

This is what the learner means by "general-purpose" prophecy. Scholars call it typological or patterned fulfilment; Willis Beecher called some prophecies "generic", one promise fulfilled in a series of events that culminate in Christ. Some Catholic scholars speak of a *sensus plenior*, a "fuller sense" intended by God beyond what the human author saw. All of these are ways of saying that God's words carry more than their first moment.

sections.heading: Conditional prophecy: when God's word is meant to change people
sections.body:
Jonah preached one sentence: "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown" (Jonah 3:4). No condition was stated. Nineveh repented, "and God repented of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did it not" (Jonah 3:10). Jonah was angry precisely because he knew God was "gracious... and repentest thee of the evil" (Jonah 4:2).

Jeremiah states the principle: if God announces disaster on a nation and it turns from evil, he will relent; if he announces blessing and it turns to evil, he will reconsider the good (Jeremiah 18:7-10). Many prophecies of judgement carry an unspoken "unless you repent". Micah's prophecy that Jerusalem would be ploughed like a field was not fulfilled in his day, and the elders later explained why: King Hezekiah feared the Lord and God relented (Jeremiah 26:18-19). Ahab's humility delayed judgement (1 Kings 21:27-29). Hezekiah was told he would die, prayed, and was given fifteen more years (2 Kings 20:1-6).

The Bible even records a prophecy adjusted in the open. Ezekiel foretold that Nebuchadnezzar would destroy Tyre (Ezekiel 26:7-14); later Ezekiel records that Nebuchadnezzar's long siege gained him nothing from Tyre, so God gave him Egypt instead (Ezekiel 29:17-20). Readers explain this differently (the prophecy was fulfilled in stages, later by Alexander; or it was conditional; or the prophet's word was revised), but the Bible does not hide it.

This matters for the test of a true prophet: "if the thing follow not, nor come to pass" (Deuteronomy 18:22). That test applies to unconditional words given as signs, not to warnings meant to produce repentance. A warning that leads to repentance has not failed; it has worked.

sections.heading: Apocalyptic: visions, symbols and four ways to read them
sections.body:
Some prophecy takes a special form called **apocalyptic** (from Greek *apokalypsis*, "unveiling"). Daniel 7–12 and Revelation are the main biblical examples. Apocalyptic writing uses dreams, angels, numbers and strange beasts to unveil what is really happening behind history: the powers that seem to rule are beasts, and God's kingdom will outlast them all (Daniel 7:13-14). Revelation says God "signified" it (Revelation 1:1): it is told in signs. Reading these symbols as newspaper code is like reading a political cartoon as a photograph.

Christians read Revelation in four main ways (see the table below). **Preterists** say most of it was fulfilled in the first century, especially the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 and Rome's persecutions. **Historicists** see it as a map of church history from the apostles to the end; this was the view of many Reformers and of Isaac Newton. **Futurists** place most of chapters 4–22 in a period still to come before Christ returns; this includes dispensationalists and many other premillennialists. **Idealists** read it as timeless pictures of the struggle between God and evil in every age. Many scholars today, such as G. K. Beale and Craig Keener, combine elements: Revelation spoke first to seven real churches, describes patterns that repeat throughout history, and looks to a real final victory.

Whatever approach you take, the centre of Revelation is the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:6). The Jesus lens matters here too: the conquering Lion of Judah turns out to be a slaughtered Lamb, and he conquers by his own blood and the faithful witness of his people (Revelation 5:5-6; Revelation 12:11).

visuals.title: What kind of prophecy is this?
visuals.intro: Choose a prophetic passage and walk it through these questions. Real passages often fit more than one category.

nodes.q: What is the prophet mainly doing in this passage?

options.label: Calling people to repent, do justice or trust God now
Remembering what God has already done
Describing visions of beasts, cosmic signs or heavenly battles

nodes.q: Is the outcome tied, openly or by implication, to how the hearers respond (a warning or an "if")?

options.label: Yes, it is a warning or promise that depends on response
No, it is given as a fixed promise or sign

nodes.q: Did it have a fulfilment in the prophet's own time or soon after?

options.label: Yes, the first hearers saw something happen
No, it points far beyond the prophet's day

nodes.q: Does the New Testament apply this passage to Jesus or the church?

options.label: Yes, as a fuller fulfilment of the same promise
Yes, as a pattern relived or repeated ("this is that")

results.title: Forth-telling
results.text: This is prophecy as God's word for the present: a call to covenant faithfulness, justice and trust. Ask what it asked of its first hearers, and what it asks of the church now. Most prophecy is of this kind.

results.title: Conditional prophecy
results.text: The word is meant to change people. If they turn, judgement may be withdrawn; if they turn away, blessing may be withdrawn. Its non-fulfilment is not failure (Jonah 3; Jeremiah 26:18-19).

results.title: Direct long-range prediction
results.text: A promise that points beyond the prophet's day to a specific fulfilment, such as Bethlehem as the birthplace of the coming ruler. Check how the New Testament reads it.

results.title: Dual or multiple fulfilment
results.text: The promise had a real meaning in its own time and a fuller meaning in Christ. Honour both: do not erase the first fulfilment, and do not stop short of the last. Example: Isaiah 7:14; 2 Samuel 7.

results.title: Patterned (typological) fulfilment
results.text: The New Testament sees God acting again in the same pattern, now at its climax in Jesus or the Spirit's outpouring. "Fulfil" here means "fill full". Examples: Hosea 11:1 in Matthew 2:15; Joel 2 in Acts 2.

results.title: Fulfilled in its own time
results.text: Many prophecies, such as oracles against Assyria or Babylon, were fulfilled in history and are not applied directly to later events. They still teach how God rules the nations and keeps his word.

results.title: Apocalyptic vision
results.text: Read the symbols as symbols. Ask what they meant to the first readers under empire, then compare the four approaches (preterist, historicist, futurist, idealist) in the table below. Keep the Lamb at the centre.

visuals.title: Isaiah 7:14: young woman or virgin?
visuals.intro: One verse, two languages, and a long debate. Each rendering is defensible; the notes show why they differ.
visuals.original: Hebrew: hinneh ha-almah harah ve-yoledet ben ve-qarat shemo Immanu-el ("Look, the young woman is pregnant / will conceive, and is bearing a son, and she will call his name Immanuel")

versions.name: Hebrew (literal)
versions.text: Behold, the young woman (almah) has conceived / will conceive and bear a son...
versions.note: Almah means a young woman of marriageable age. It does not by itself stress virginity (the more specific word is betulah), though an almah would normally be unmarried and a virgin in that culture.

versions.name: Greek Septuagint (2nd–3rd century BC)
versions.note: Jewish translators before Jesus rendered almah with parthenos, usually "virgin". Matthew quotes this Greek form.

versions.name: Matthew 1:23
versions.text: Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us.
versions.note: Matthew sees the fullest meaning of the sign in Jesus' virgin birth and translates the name: God with us.

versions.name: KJV (1611); NIV; ESV
versions.text: Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
versions.note: Follows Matthew's reading and the church's tradition.

versions.name: RSV (1952); NRSV; NET
versions.text: Behold, a young woman shall conceive and bear a son... / this young woman is about to conceive...
versions.note: Follows the Hebrew word's normal meaning. The RSV's choice caused heated controversy in 1952; translators replied that Matthew's use of the Greek is still affirmed.

versions.name: Jewish Publication Society Tanakh
versions.text: Look, the young woman is with child and about to give birth to a son...
versions.note: Jewish translation, reading the sign as fulfilled in Ahaz's own day.

visuals.title: Four (and a half) ways to read Revelation

rows.label: Preterist (partial)
cells: Most of Revelation was fulfilled in the first century (the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, Rome's persecutions); the final return of Christ is still future.
Rev 1:1; Rev 1:3; Rev 22:10; Matt 24:34
Luis de Alcázar (1614); Kenneth Gentry; R. C. Sproul
Takes seriously "the time is at hand" and the first readers' situation.
Can make the book seem to have little to say about the future. Its dating often depends on an early date for Revelation.

rows.label: Full preterist
cells: All prophecy, including Christ's return and the resurrection, was fulfilled by AD 70.
Matt 16:28; Matt 24:34
A small modern minority
Consistent with time statements.
Rejected by all the historic creeds, which confess a future return and resurrection.

rows.label: Historicist
cells: Revelation maps church history from the apostles to the end, often identifying the papacy or other powers with the beast.
Dan 7:25; Rev 13; Rev 17
Many Reformers; Isaac Newton; early Seventh-day Adventists
Gives the book meaning for every generation of the church.
Interpreters constantly revise the map as history moves on; it tends to centre on Western Europe.

rows.label: Futurist
cells: Most of chapters 4–22 describe events still to come before Christ's return.
Francisco Ribera (1590); dispensationalists (Darby, Scofield); historic premillennialists (George Ladd)
Takes the book's future hope literally and seriously.
Can make most of the book irrelevant to its first readers and encourage date-setting.

rows.label: Idealist
cells: Timeless symbolic pictures of the battle between God and evil in every age, ending in God's victory.
Influenced by Tyconius and Augustine; William Hendriksen (More Than Conquerors)
Speaks to every church in every age.
May lose the book's real history and its concrete hope of a final end.

rows.label: Eclectic
cells: Combines elements: first-century message, repeating patterns, a real future climax.
G. K. Beale; Craig Keener; many recent commentators
Draws on the strengths of each approach.
Critics say it can be vague about which parts belong where.

voices.text: Every prophecy, before its fulfilment, is to men full of enigmas and ambiguities. But when the time has arrived, and the prediction has come to pass, then the prophecies have a clear and certain exposition.

views.name: Christ-centred fulfilment (the Jesus lens)
views.who: The learner; Greg Boyd; Brian Zahnd; much of the early church (Irenaeus, Augustine)
views.summary: All prophecy finds its "yes" in Jesus (2 Cor 1:20). The point of prophecy is not a timetable but a person: "the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy" (Rev 19:10). Read even the hardest visions through the Lamb who was slain.
views.strengths: It follows the apostles' own way of reading (Luke 24:27; Acts 2). It protects against fear-driven end-times speculation.
views.critiques: Some say it can flatten prophecy's original meaning for Israel and its real future predictions. Futurists say it can spiritualise promises God means literally.

views.name: Grammatical-historical with dual fulfilment
views.who: Many evangelical scholars (e.g. Walter Kaiser, though he prefers "single meaning" with a generic fulfilment; Willis Beecher)
views.summary: Start with what the prophet meant to his hearers. Where the New Testament applies a prophecy to Christ, see either one promise with a series of fulfilments (generic) or a near and far fulfilment.
views.strengths: It protects the original meaning and history of each prophecy while honouring the New Testament.
views.critiques: Critics say it can force Matthew's patterned readings into a prediction framework that does not fit, as with Hos 11:1.

views.name: Sensus plenior (fuller sense)
views.who: Raymond Brown (on sensus plenior, 1955); many Catholic interpreters
views.summary: God, the primary author of Scripture, intended a fuller meaning than the human prophet consciously grasped, which becomes clear in later revelation.
views.strengths: It explains how New Testament fulfilments can go beyond what the original author saw.
views.critiques: Critics ask how we can control a meaning the author did not intend; it can open the door to arbitrary readings unless guided by the New Testament and the church.

views.name: Dispensational futurism
views.who: John Nelson Darby; C. I. Scofield; Charles Ryrie; John Walvoord
views.summary: Prophecy should be read as literally as possible. Many promises to Israel and many prophecies in Daniel and Revelation await future, literal fulfilment, distinct from the church.
views.strengths: It takes God's promises to Israel seriously and expects a real future for history.
views.critiques: Others say it underplays the New Testament's own patterned fulfilments and has fuelled repeated failed date-setting. Progressive dispensationalists have softened several of these points.

views.name: Historical-critical
views.who: Many academic scholars (e.g. John J. Collins on apocalyptic)
views.summary: Prophecies are best understood in their own historical settings. Daniel 7–12, for example, is usually dated by these scholars to around 165 BC under Antiochus IV, so its "predictions" are largely history told as prophecy. New Testament fulfilments are the early church's creative rereading.
views.strengths: It pays close attention to history and genre and explains apocalyptic symbols well.
views.critiques: Traditional scholars argue for a 6th-century date for Daniel and say the method rules out real prediction in advance. Believers note that it says little about how God speaks through the text now.

misreadings.topic: "Prophecy is mainly about predicting the end times"
misreadings.popular: Many Christians meet prophecy mainly through end-times charts, news-watching and predictions about current events.
misreadings.inContext: Most biblical prophecy addressed the prophets' own generation, calling Israel back to covenant faithfulness, justice and trust. Even Revelation was written to seven real churches facing pressure under Rome (Rev 1:4; Rev 2–3).
misreadings.defence: Futurist scholars agree that most prophecy is forth-telling. They hold that some prophecy still concerns the future and that expecting Christ's return is biblical (Acts 1:11; 1 Thess 4:16-17), while warning against date-setting (Matt 24:36).
misreadings.whyItMatters: Reading prophecy as a timetable produces fear and failed predictions; reading it as covenant speech produces repentance, justice and hope.

misreadings.popular: Some readers (both sceptics and new believers) think Matthew pulled verses like Hosea 11:1 out of context to prove Jesus was the Messiah.
misreadings.inContext: Matthew knew Hosea 11:1 was about the exodus. His point is that Jesus relives Israel's story as God's faithful Son. "Fulfil" means "fill full". This is a recognised Jewish way of reading patterns, not a mistake.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars and many non-evangelical scholars agree that Matthew reads typologically. Critical scholars still note that Matthew's method differs from modern historical exegesis.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Understanding patterned fulfilment helps us read the New Testament's use of the Old with confidence and trains us to see Jesus as the climax of Israel's story.

discuss: Read Jonah 3–4. Was Jonah a false prophet because Nineveh was not destroyed? What does Jeremiah 18:7-10 add?
Isaiah 7:14 had to mean something to King Ahaz. How does that change the way you hear it at Christmas?
Peter says "this is that" at Pentecost. Where might the church today rightly say "this is that", and where might it be overreaching?
Which of the four ways of reading Revelation have you met? What did it produce in the people who held it: fear, hope, faithfulness?
If most prophecy is forth-telling, what might a prophetic word to your church or city sound like today?
practice: Read Hosea 11:1-4 and then Matthew 2:13-15 and Matthew 4:1-11. List every way Jesus relives Israel's story.
Pick three prophecies (for example Micah 5:2, Jonah 3:4 and Joel 2:28) and run each through the decision tree. Note where you were unsure.
Read Revelation 4–5 aloud. Notice where the Lion is announced and the Lamb appears. Write one sentence on what this says about how God wins.
